stem: A patient who lost weight rapidly on Mounjaro (tirzepatide) has abdominal distension relieved by vomiting. What is the cause?
ansText: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome — rapid weight loss shrinks the mesenteric fat pad, so the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA (in front) and the aorta (behind). (The source wrote it the other way round — the SMA compresses the duodenum.)

stem: A 50-year-old lady who failed multiple medically supervised weight loss programs, presents to the clinic for Bariatric Surgery, she is healthy except for 2-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, she has esophagitis on endoscopy and dependent on proton pump inhibitor. Which Bariatric Procedure would you recommend for this patient?
srcNote: (Obesity and bariatric surgery) Source note (Final 436 A Q24): The related comorbidity-selection question keys "Gastroesophageal reflux disease" and states: "answer is confirmed when Q was reviewed with the course organiser."
expl: Obesity with GERD and oesophagitis on PPIs → Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. It relieves reflux (small pouch with little acid, bile diverted), whereas a sleeve worsens reflux — severe oesophagitis contraindicates the sleeve.

why.A: The sleeve is a high-pressure tube that worsens GERD.
why.B: A balloon gives temporary, modest weight loss and doesn't treat GERD.
why.D: The band has a high failure rate and can worsen reflux.

stem: A patient post gastric sleeve developed tachycardia and decreased urine output. Which one of the following is the reason?
srcNote: Source note (Final 439 A Q24): The related recall describes signs of septic shock and keys option C, written as "Stable leak" in that source.
expl: Tachycardia (often the earliest sign) and falling urine output after sleeve gastrectomy → staple-line leak until proven otherwise.

why.A: Possible, but tachycardia after sleeve = leak classically.
why.D: Later and milder.

stem: 42 years old female who underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy 3 years ago. Has experienced regaining her weight. She originally lost weight and had good initial weight loss (BMI reduced from 52 to 40). Then she experienced heartburn and her BMI is currently 48. GI contrast study and endoscopy confirmed a stricture in the mid portion of the gastric pouch with a dilation of gastric fundus with severe GERD. What is the appropriate management?
expl: A failed sleeve with weight regain, stricture, dilated fundus and severe GERD → convert to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. It treats the reflux, bypasses the stricture and gives further weight loss.

why.A: Dilating the stricture leaves the severe GERD and the regain untreated.
why.D: Resecting the fundus is a re-sleeve — same problem.

stem: Patient who underwent gastric bypass 2 months ago has developed symptoms of obstruction What is the most common cause besides adhesions
srcNote: From AMBOSS:Patients with a history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or liver transplant are especially at risk of internal hernia formation. Small bowel loops are the most common content of an internal hernia. For this reason, the typical clinical presentation is that of a mechanical small bowel obstruction.
expl: After Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, internal hernia (through Petersen's or the mesenteric defects, especially with weight loss) is the most common cause of SBO besides adhesions — it can strangulate, so operate early.

why.A: Incisional hernias are uncommon after laparoscopy.
why.C: Malignancy is rare 2 months after surgery.
why.D: SMA syndrome causes duodenal obstruction with rapid weight loss — much rarer.

stem: which one of the following is an absolute contraindication for bariatric surgery?

opts.t: Failure to reduce weight before surgery

expl: Keyed answer: psychological disturbance (untreated psychiatric illness — binge eating, substance abuse, severe depression) is a contraindication because the patient can't comply with lifelong changes. Age < 18 isn't absolute (adolescent bariatric surgery is done in selected cases).

why.A: Not absolute — adolescents can be operated on in selected centres.
why.C: Abnormal eating habits are treated/assessed but aren't absolute.
why.D: Failing to lose weight before surgery is why surgery is offered.

stem: Why are obese patients at increased risk of complications during surgery? (Only one option survived in the source.)

opts.t: Procedures could take a longer time

srcNote: (Miscellaneous) Incomplete choice set: options B, C and D are blank in the source.
ansText: Keyed: procedures can take longer (technically harder access and exposure). Other reasons: difficult airway and ventilation (OSA, low lung reserve), VTE, wound infection and dehiscence, cardiovascular disease, positioning injuries.

stem: In morbid obesity, All could be a complication of OSA except:
expl: OSA → repeated apnoea → hypoxia and CO₂ retention (hypercarbia, not hypocarbia) → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure; systemic hypertension → LV failure.

why.A: A complication.
why.D: Correct — the exception (OSA causes hypercarbia).

stem: Which of the following groups has the highest prevalence of obesity worldwide?
expl: Keyed answer: in Western (high-income) countries obesity is most prevalent in low socioeconomic groups — cheap calorie-dense food, less physical activity.

why.A: Childhood obesity is rising fast, but adults have the higher prevalence.
why.C: Asian populations have the lowest rates (though more metabolic risk at a lower BMI).
why.D: A sex ratio is not a population group (women have slightly higher rates).

stem: The basal metabolic rate of an obese person in comparison to a normal weight person (same age and gender)?
expl: The absolute basal metabolic rate rises with body size — an obese person has more lean mass (and fat) to maintain, so their BMR is higher than a normal-weight person of the same age and sex. Obesity comes from intake exceeding expenditure, not a low BMR.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: A common myth — absolute BMR is higher.
why.D: Genetics affects weight but isn't an answer to the comparison.

stem: Obese patient what investigation you direct toward
srcNote: (Obesity surgery) Incomplete choice set: option D is blank in the source.
expl: Work-up before bariatric surgery aims to detect and optimise obesity-related comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension, OSA, GERD, gallstones, dyslipidaemia) — they decide eligibility and peri-operative risk.

why.A: Endocrine causes (hypothyroidism, Cushing's) are excluded, but they are rare.
why.C: The type of surgery is chosen from the history and comorbidities, not targeted investigations.

stem: which of the following is the correct way to measure BMI?
expl: BMI = weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared (kg/m²).

why.A: Height must be squared.
why.D: Correct.

stem: Patient did a sleeve gastrectomy surgery case, 1 week later developed overt gastric leak. Hemodynamically unstable, peritonitis symptoms and signs. after resuscitation and stabilizing what’s the most appropriate management?

opts.t: percutaneous drainage and control of leak.
surgical control of leak, local irrigation, and appropriate drainage

expl: An overt leak with peritonitis in an unstable patient → after resuscitation, surgical control: washout, drainage ± repair. Stents/percutaneous drainage are for stable patients with contained leaks.

why.A: For stable, contained leaks.
why.D: Correct.

stem: A 35-year-old man came to the emergency department complaining of persistent hiccups. He had undergone sleeve gastrectomy 10 days ago. His vital signs were HR: 112,BP 99/60, 02 Sat 99% on Room Air, Temp: 39C What is the best next step in his management following resuscitation?

opts.t: Reassure patient that hiccups are expected and will go away
Consult pulmonology to manage his hiccups
Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen to rule out leak or abscess
Prescribe chlorpromazine and discharge the patient

expl: Fever, tachycardia and hiccups (diaphragmatic irritation) after sleeve gastrectomy suggest a staple-line leak/subphrenic abscess → CT abdomen.

why.A: Dangerous.
why.D: Dangerous.

stem: a 45-year-old lady underwent laparoscopic roux-en-y gastric bypass (LRYGB) 4 weeks prior, presenting complaining of on and off agonizing epigastric pain with occasional bloody stained vomiting. On examination, vital signs are within normal, and her abdomen is soft What is the appropriate investigation at this stage?
expl: Epigastric pain with blood-stained vomiting weeks after RYGB in a stable patient → marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunostomy → upper GI endoscopy (diagnoses and can treat it).

why.A: Correct.
why.B: A barium meal can't see a mucosal ulcer well or treat it.
why.C: CT is for obstruction/internal hernia/leak; the vomited blood points to a mucosal lesion.
why.D: US looks at the gallbladder.

stem: A patient underwent a gastric sleeve surgery 2 years prior and presents today with symptoms of hyperparathyroidism. What is the likely cause?
expl: Sleeve gastrectomy/bariatric surgery reduces calcium and vitamin D absorption → vitamin D deficiency → secondary hyperparathyroidism.

why.A: Not related.
why.C: A consequence of PTH, not a cause.
why.D: Low magnesium suppresses PTH.

stem: A 40 Year-old obese male was booked for a day surgery, anesthetic review preopertively assesed him as (low to intermediate risk),which of the following is the most likely cause?
srcNote: (not sure) (Pre-Operative Assessment) Uncertain source key: the original answer is marked "not sure".
expl: BMI 30–40 = mild systemic disease (ASA II) → low-to-intermediate risk; that is why he was rated so. Age 40 isn't a risk factor by itself.

why.A: ASA 3 would be higher risk.
why.D: Age 40 is not a significant risk factor.

stem: 50 year old patient post Roux-e-Y procedure after 4 years he came with severe colics in the center of the abdomen he was hemodynamically stable and all his vitals were alright. Which of the following is most commonly the cause of his presentation?
expl: Source key: adhesions (commonest cause of SBO after any abdominal surgery). After Roux-en-Y, internal hernia is the classic special concern for intermittent colicky pain.

why.A: Important differential after RYGB.
why.D: Marginal ulcer causes epigastric pain, not colic.

stem: Patient done Roux-e-Y procedure and after a while presented with symptoms of marginal ulcer what’s the most common cause of that?
expl: Marginal ulcers at the gastrojejunal anastomosis after Roux-en-Y bypass are mostly caused by NSAIDs (and smoking) — patients are told to avoid NSAIDs for life.

why.A: Acetaminophen is the safe analgesic after bypass.
why.C: Warfarin increases bleeding but doesn't cause ulcers.
why.D: Hydroxyurea is not linked to marginal ulcers.

stem: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department 5 weeks post laparoscopic gastric bypass, complaining of inability to tolerate food. He explained that he was able to tolerate diet up to a week before his presentation when he developed difficulty tolerating solid food and now progressed to inability to tolerate liquid diet. What is the most likely cause for this patient's inability to tolerate solid and liquid diet?
expl: Weeks after bypass, progressive intolerance — first solids, then liquids — is the classic story of a gastrojejunal anastomotic stricture (narrowing). Treated with endoscopic balloon dilatation.

why.A: Internal hernia causes colicky pain with intermittent obstruction, not steady progressive dysphagia.
why.B: Intussusception is rare and gives colicky pain.
why.D: Adhesions cause SBO with distension and colic.

stem: A young female came 3 years post-sleeve, complaining of RUQ abdominal pain and jaundice. her labs GGT 450, APT 630, Amylase normal, total bilirubin 200, direct bilirubin 120. The US abdomen showed stones in the gallbladder and CBD measuring 11mm. What’s the best management for her ?
expl: Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice (CBD 11 mm) → clear the duct with ERCP first, then cholecystectomy (same admission). After a sleeve the anatomy still lets the endoscope reach the papilla — unlike after RYGB.

why.A: Correct.
why.B: Leaves the obstructed CBD for later — the duct should be cleared first.
why.C: Cholecystectomy alone doesn't clear the CBD stones.
why.D: She is obstructed (bilirubin 200) — needs drainage, not observation.

stem: A 25-year-old man who underwent sleeve gastrectomy for morbid obesity. 7 days ago he developed gastric fistula with output of 250 ml/day. Which of the following is the most frequently associated with this condition?
srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients)
expl: Gastric juice is rich in H⁺, Cl⁻ and K⁺; a gastric fistula causes hypokalaemia with hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (plus renal K⁺ loss from volume depletion/aldosterone).

why.A: Urinary K may rise, but the keyed finding is hypokalaemia.
why.D: Correct.

stem: Which of the following is a complication of obesity surgery?
srcNote: (Upper gastrointestinal and bariatric surgery, abdominal wall, umbilicus, herniae, and retroperitoneum), This is because as the body metabolises fat during rapid Weight Loss, it causes the liver to secrete extra cholesterol into the bile, potentially causing gallstones. Year not stated
expl: Rapid weight loss after bariatric surgery raises biliary cholesterol → gallstones. Diabetes, hypertension and hypothyroidism improve or aren't caused.

why.A: Correct.
why.D: Hypertension improves.

stem: Roux-en-y gastric bypass is an indication of which of the following comorbidities?
expl: RYGB has the strongest metabolic effect (incretin/hormonal changes) — the operation of choice for obese patients with type 2 diabetes. The source's lowercase key "b" = DM.

why.A: Sleep apnea improves with any weight loss — it doesn't specifically need RYGB.
why.C: Hypertension improves with any weight loss.
why.D: Osteoarthritis improves with any weight loss.
